opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we've thought about a lot. The key insight is that a relational database isn't just a bunch of separate tables. It's really a graph. Every row is an entity, like a customer, a product, or a transaction, and the primary and foreign key relationships tell you how those entities connect. So when we say a relational foundation model generalizes to a database it's never seen, part of what that means is it has learned to reason over the *structure* of these relational graphs, not over one specific schema.

There are a few ingredients that make this work. The first is representation. You need to encode heterogeneous data, like numbers, categories, text, and timestamps, in a way that's schema-agnostic. The model shouldn't care that a column is called "price" in one database and "amount" in another. It needs a general way of turning a cell, a row, and its neighborhood into something it can reason about.

The second is the architecture. We use graph-based attention, essentially a graph transformer, that can attend across tables by following those key relationships. The model learns patterns like "entities that have a lot of recent activity linked to them behave differently from entities that have gone quiet." Those kinds of patterns show up again and again across domains, whether you're predicting churn in e-commerce, fraud in finance, or readmission in healthcare.

The third piece, and I think the most important one, is in-context learning. Rather than retraining for every new task, you give the model labeled examples from the new database at prediction time, like "here are some customers who churned and some who didn't." The model then figures out what distinguishes them by looking at their relational context. It's very analogous to how large language models do few-shot learning, except the "prompt" is a set of subgraphs from your database.

And then time matters enormously. Predictions on databases are almost always about the future, so the model has to respect temporal ordering. It only looks at information available before the prediction time. That makes the learned patterns causal in the right direction and prevents leakage, which is a big reason why these models transfer well instead of just memorizing.

So when people ask what lets the model work on unseen data, my answer is that it has learned a kind of universal grammar of relational data. Across thousands of tasks and databases, the same structural and temporal motifs keep recurring, and once you pretrain on enough of that diversity, a new database starts to look less like something foreign and more like a new instance of patterns the model already understands.

r001.rationale: The response discusses schema-agnostic encoding of numbers and reasoning over relational structure, but does not say the model identifies relevant relationships among previously unseen numbers.

r002.rationale: The response says labeled examples are provided at prediction time to form a prompt, but does not describe querying for relevant examples to construct that context.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the question, right? Because when you think about it, every database is different. Different tables, different columns, different schema, different domain. One is an e-commerce database, another is a hospital, another is a bank. So how can one model make predictions on a database it has literally never seen?

The way I think about it is that there are actually a few things going on. The first is that we don't treat the database as a collection of tables. We treat it as a graph. Every row becomes a node, and every foreign key, every primary key to foreign key link, becomes an edge. And once you do that, something interesting happens. The schema disappears in a sense. A customer connected to orders connected to products looks, structurally, a lot like a patient connected to visits connected to diagnoses. The names are different, but the relational structure, the patterns of how entities connect to each other over time, those are shared across domains.

The second piece is how we represent the values themselves. A model trained on one database would learn, say, that column number seven means something specific. That doesn't transfer. So instead, we encode cells by their type and content: numbers, categories, text, timestamps. We use things like pretrained text encoders for the textual parts. So the model is never memorizing "this column," it's learning what a number looks like, what a time looks like, what a piece of text means, independently of where it sits in a schema.

And then the third piece, which I think is the most important, is in-context learning. Rather than fine-tuning for every new task, we show the model examples at inference time. Here are entities, here is their history up to some point in time, here is what happened to them afterward. And the model has to figure out, from those examples, what the task is and what the predictive signal is. So the model is really learning to learn from relational context. We pretrain it on many synthetic and real databases with many different tasks, so it has seen an enormous variety of structures and prediction problems, and at test time it generalizes to a new one.

So when I ask myself what enables the generalization, it's that combination. The graph representation gives you structural transfer. The cell-level encoding gives you value-level transfer. And the in-context setup gives you task-level transfer. And honestly, part of the answer is also empirical. We were somewhat surprised ourselves at how well it works. You take a database it has never seen, you give it a handful of labeled examples, and it's competitive with or better than models that were trained specifically on that database with full supervision. That tells me there is a lot of shared structure in relational data that we as a community had not really been exploiting.

r001.rationale: The response describes representing rows as graph nodes and links as edges, and encoding numeric cells by type and content. It does not say the model identifies relevant relationships among previously unseen numbers.

r002.rationale: The response says examples are shown at inference time to provide context, but does not describe querying for relevant examples to construct that context.

astra-6.text:
The key is that, although a database may be new, the relationships it contains can have patterns that are familiar. Think about a customer, the products they buy, and the transactions connecting them. The names of the tables and columns might change across databases, but the predictive structure can be similar.

A relational model can represent rows as nodes and connections between rows as edges. To make a prediction about a particular customer, it gathers information from the related transactions, products, and other relevant records. So it learns both how to interpret the information in a row and how to combine information across relationships.

What we want a relational foundation model to learn during pretraining is a transferable way of doing that. Rather than memorizing a particular database, it learns patterns that can be useful in a new database, given its schema, its data, and the prediction task. That doesn’t mean it can predict anything from any database automatically. The important question is how well those learned patterns transfer when the entities, relationships, or tasks change.

r002.rationale: It describes gathering information from related records, but does not describe querying relevant examples to construct the model’s inference context.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that a relational database gives you more than individual data points. It gives you relationships. A customer is connected to purchases, purchases are connected to products, and those connections provide context for making a prediction.

A relational foundation model can learn how to use that context across many prediction tasks. Instead of learning a separate model for every table and every target, you're learning a shared way to combine information from an entity and its neighborhood. When a new customer or a new purchase appears, the model can apply that same computation to the new data.

Now, there's an important distinction between new rows in a database and an entirely new database. For new rows, you can reuse the structure and patterns you've already learned. For a new database, the challenge is harder: the tables, columns, and meanings may all be different. So the question is how much of what the model has learned is a general strategy for using relational information, and how much is specific to the database it was trained on. That's really what determines its ability to generalize.

r001.rationale: The response says relational connections provide context and that learned patterns can apply to new rows, but it does not clearly attribute prediction on unseen data to identifying relevant relationships among previously unseen numbers.

r002.rationale: It describes combining information from an entity and its neighborhood, but does not mention querying relevant examples to construct inference context.
